For **thin lenses in contact** the powers simply add, whichever way round the curved
faces point.
**Step 1 — state the rule.**
1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ ✓
for thin lenses touching, independent of how they are oriented.
**Step 2 — apply it to each arrangement.** Each lens has focal length f, so in **all
three** cases
1/F = 1/f + 1/f = 2/f
**F = f/2** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
F₁ : F₂ : F₃ = **1 : 1 : 1** ✓
**Why the orientation makes no difference.** A thin lens's focal length depends only on
**(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)**, and turning the lens round swaps and re-signs the radii in a way that
leaves that combination unchanged ✓ A plano-convex lens has the same focal length
whichever face the light strikes first.
**Checking with the lens-maker's formula.** For a plano-convex lens of radius R:
curved face first: (n − 1)(1/R − 1/∞) = **(n − 1)/R**
flat face first: (n − 1)(1/∞ − 1/(−R)) = **(n − 1)/R** ✓ identical.
**What the three arrangements do differ in.** Not the focal length, but the
**aberrations** ✓ The arrangement with the curved faces **outward** - the biconvex
configuration - shares the bending between two surfaces and suffers the least
**spherical aberration**. That is why a plano-convex lens used alone is oriented with
its curved face towards the parallel beam.
**A worked instance.** Two lenses of f = 20 cm in contact:
P = 5 + 5 = **10 D**, so F = **10 cm** ✓ in every arrangement.
**Why "thin" and "in contact" matter.** Separate the lenses by d and the formula gains
a term:
1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ − **d/(f₁f₂)** ✓
and then the arrangement does affect the result - but only through the separation, not
through the orientation.
**A note on the gap between the faces.** In arrangements (i) and (iii) the curved
surfaces leave an air gap ✓ For truly thin lenses that gap is negligible; were it
filled with a liquid, a third lens would be created and the answer would change.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 2 : 1**, **3 : 2 : 1** and **1 : 2 : 3** ✗ all
suppose the orientation changes the power ✓ The lens-maker's formula shows it does not.
∴ 1 : 1 : 1.

The **number of waves** in a fixed distance is inversely proportional to the wavelength,
and wavelength is inversely proportional to the refractive index.
**Step 1 — write the wave counts.** Over the same distance D,
x = D/λ₁ and y = D/λ₂ ✓
**Step 2 — invert for the wavelengths.**
λ₁ = D/x and λ₂ = D/y ✓
**Step 3 — relate wavelength to refractive index.** The **frequency** is unchanged when
light crosses a boundary, so
nλ = constant ✓ giving **n₁λ₁ = n₂λ₂**
**Step 4 — form the required ratio.**
n₁/n₂ = λ₂/λ₁
= (D/y)/(D/x)
= **x/y** ✓
**Why the frequency stays fixed.** It is set by the **source**, and the boundary cannot
create or destroy wave crests ✓ Whatever arrives must leave at the same rate - so when
the speed changes, the **wavelength** must change to match.
**The chain of relations.**
v = c/n, and v = fλ with f fixed, so **λ ∝ 1/n** ✓
A denser medium means a shorter wavelength and therefore **more** waves packed into the
same distance.
**A sanity check on the answer.** If medium A is denser, n₁ > n₂, so λ₁ < λ₂ and **more**
waves fit into the distance: x > y ✓ The ratio x/y is then greater than 1, matching
n₁/n₂ > 1. The formula behaves correctly.
**A worked instance.** Light of 600 nm in air entering glass of n = 1·5:
in air: λ = 600 nm, so over 6 µm there are **10** waves ✓
in glass: λ = 400 nm, so over 6 µm there are **15** ✓
n_air/n_glass = 1/1·5 = **0·667**, and x/y = 10/15 = **0·667** ✓ exact.
**Why the colour appears unchanged.** Perceived colour follows the **frequency**, not
the wavelength ✓ which is why a diver sees objects in their proper colours even though
every wavelength has shrunk by a factor of 4/3.
**Reading the distractors.** **y/x** ✗ inverts the ratio - it would be n₂/n₁. **√(x/y)**
✗ introduces a square root with no basis, and **x/(y − x)** ✗ matches no relation ✓ A
dimensional check is no help here, since all are pure numbers; the physics must be
followed through.
∴ x/y.

Normal shift **increases** with refractive index, so the statement that it decreases is
the wrong one.
**Step 1 — write the normal shift.** For a slab of thickness t viewed normally, the
apparent position of an object beneath it is raised by
**shift = t(1 − 1/n)** ✓
**Step 2 — see how it varies with n.** As n grows, 1/n shrinks, so (1 − 1/n) **grows** ✓
shift
n = 1·33: t(1 − 0·75) = **0·25t**
n = 1·5: **0·33t**
n = 2·0: **0·50t** ✓
The shift plainly **increases** with n - so the third statement is **false** ✓
**Step 3 — check the other three.**
"**lateral shift increases with the angle of incidence**" ✓ **true** - from
shift = t sin(i − r)/cos r, which rises from zero at normal incidence towards t as
i → 90°.
"**lateral shift increases with refractive index**" ✓ **true** - a larger n bends the
ray more, increasing (i − r) and hence the displacement.
"**both shifts are proportional to the thickness**" ✓ **true** - t appears as a simple
factor in both formulas.
**The two shifts distinguished.**
**normal shift** - the apparent **raising** of an object seen through the slab, along
the line of sight ✓ t(1 − 1/n)
**lateral shift** - the sideways **displacement** of an obliquely incident ray, which
emerges parallel to its original direction ✓ t sin(i − r)/cos r
**A worked instance.** A 6 cm glass slab, n = 1·5:
normal shift = 6(1 − 2/3) = **2 cm** ✓ an object below appears 2 cm nearer
lateral shift at 60° incidence: r = 35·3°, so 6 sin(24·7°)/cos(35·3°) = **3·07 cm** ✓
**The limits of the normal shift.**
n → 1: shift → **0** ✓ no slab effect at all
n → ∞: shift → **t**, the object appearing to rise to the slab's top surface ✓
It can never exceed t, which is itself a useful check.
**Why the apparent depth falls while the shift rises.** apparent depth = t/n **falls**
with n, and the shift t − t/n correspondingly **rises** ✓ The two are complementary, and
confusing them is exactly what the false statement invites.
∴ the statement that normal shift decreases as the refractive index increases.

Total internal reflection requires light to go from **denser to rarer** and to strike
the boundary beyond the **critical angle**.
**Step 1 — find the two refractive indices.**
n₁ = c/v₁ = (3 x 10⁸)/(1·5 x 10⁸) = **2** ✓
n₂ = c/v₂ = (3 x 10⁸)/(2 x 10⁸) = **1·5** ✓
**Step 2 — check the direction.** The ray goes from M₁ (n = 2) to M₂ (n = 1·5), that is
from **denser to rarer** ✓ so total internal reflection is possible.
**Step 3 — find the critical angle.**
sin C = n₂/n₁
= 1·5/2
= **3/4** ✓
**C = sin⁻¹(3/4) = 48·6°**
**Step 4 — state the condition.** TIR occurs for angles of incidence **greater** than
the critical angle:
**θ > sin⁻¹(3/4)** ✓
**Why "greater than" and not "greater than or equal to".** At exactly the critical angle
the refracted ray **grazes** along the surface, at 90° ✓ The reflection becomes total
only **beyond** it, which is why the strict inequality is the right answer and the
option with ≤ is wrong twice over.
**Why the slower medium is the denser one.** n = c/v, so a smaller speed means a larger
index ✓ Light travels at 1·5 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in M₁ - half its vacuum speed - making M₁ an
unusually dense medium, denser than diamond's 1·24 x 10⁸.
**What happens below the critical angle.** The light **refracts** out into M₂, bending
**away** from the normal, with a partial reflection as well ✓ As θ approaches C, more
and more goes into the reflected beam, until at C the refracted beam vanishes entirely.
**Where TIR is used.** **Optical fibres**, where light is trapped in the core by
repeated total reflection; **prismatic binoculars**; **periscopes**; and the sparkle of
a **diamond**, whose critical angle of 24° traps light through many internal bounces ✓
**Why it is called "total".** Unlike ordinary reflection, which returns only a few per
cent, TIR returns **100%** of the light ✓ There is no absorption and no transmitted
beam - which is why fibre links can run for kilometres.
**Reading the distractors.** "**< sin⁻¹(3/4)**" ✗ is the refracting range. "**= sin⁻¹(4/3)**"
✗ is impossible, since 4/3 exceeds 1 and has no inverse sine. "**≤ sin⁻¹(3/4)**" ✗
wrongly includes the grazing case ✓
∴ > sin⁻¹(3/4).

Apply the lens-maker's formula with the radii in the ratio **1 : 2** for a converging
lens.
**Step 1 — assign the radii.** For a biconvex converging lens with the first surface of
radius R and the second of radius 2R, the sign convention gives
R₁ = **+R** and R₂ = **−2R** ✓
**Step 2 — write the lens-maker's formula.**
1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
= (1·5 − 1)[1/R − 1/(−2R)]
= 0·5(1/R + 1/2R) ✓
**Step 3 — simplify the bracket.**
1/R + 1/2R = **3/(2R)**
so
1/f = 0·5 x 3/(2R)
= **3/(4R)** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute f = 6 cm.**
1/6 = 3/(4R)
4R = 18
**R = 4·5 cm** ✓
**Step 5 — state both radii.**
**4·5 cm and 9 cm** ✓
**Step 6 — verify.**
1/f = 0·5(1/4·5 + 1/9) = 0·5(0·2222 + 0·1111) = 0·5(0·3333) = **0·1667** ✓
f = **6 cm** ✓ exactly as given.
**Why R₂ is negative.** With light travelling left to right, a surface **bulging
towards** the incoming light has a positive radius and one bulging **away** a negative
one ✓ For a biconvex lens the two signs are opposite, which is why the bracket becomes a
**sum** and the lens converges.
**Why both radii must be smaller than the focal length here.** The bracket
(n − 1) = 0·5 is only a half, so the surfaces must curve quite sharply to give a 6 cm
focal length ✓ With n = 1·5, a lens's focal length is always roughly twice its radius of
curvature.
**The equiconvex check.** If both radii were equal to R:
1/f = 0·5(2/R) = 1/R, so **f = R** ✓ For f = 6 cm that would need R = 6 cm - which is
the second distractor, and what one gets by ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio.
**Reading the other distractors.** **9 and 18 cm** ✗ and **3 and 6 cm** ✗ give focal
lengths of 12 cm and 4 cm respectively ✓ Substituting each pair into the lens-maker's
formula tests it in one line.
∴ 4.5 cm and 9 cm.
